Okay, you're on.
Do you want to start out by identifying yourself?
I'm Glenn Dennis.
You live where, Glenn?
Roswell, New Mexico.
And the date is?
I have no idea what it is.
Can we get an age from you?
I'm 66 years old.
Okay. How did you first become involved in this?
The way I first became involved, I got a call. I was employed at the time at the Ballard Field in Roswell, New Mexico.
As a what?
I'm sorry?
mortician. We had the contract for the base at the Roswell Army Airfield. We had the contract
for all of the mortuary services. I got a call about around 1-15, or somewhere right
after lunch, around 1-15 or 1-30, from the mortuary officer wanting to know what size,
what was the smallest size hermetically sealed casket that we had in Stockton that we could get.
And I think I informed him that we usually kept a four foot, but I could possibly get a three six.
And I said, I mean, what do you have in mind?
He said, well, this would be for future services later on in case we, he said,
He said, we need to know this in case something comes up in the future.
Do you recall his name?
No, I don't recall his name.
I had at the time, Stan Friedman and I went over to check the records,
but I couldn't find the name, and I don't remember the name.
But anyway, I told him, he said, well, how long would it take you to get if we needed more than one?
because we always just kept a four-foot in stock.
And I said, if you call me by 3 o'clock in the afternoon,
I can have it in here by 7 the next morning
because they come from Amarillo, Texas.
And he said, okay, we'll talk to you later.
Glenn, had you gotten requests like that before?
No, not necessarily.
Usually, you know, people, until they really have a need for it,
you don't ever have a call for it.
There's very few at that time, pre-need services weren't too popular at that time.
Then about another hour, maybe 45 minutes later, I get a call from the same officer.
He said, I would like to know what your preparations for bodies that might have been laying out in the elements are.
He said, could you give me what your preparation and how you would do it.
And then before I could explain our procedure, before I could explain it, he said what we're
interested in, and this would probably be for future use too, he said, would your procedure,
what you would have to do to the bodies that have been exposed to the elements and everything,
what would your procedure do to changing the chemical compounds, the tissues, the blood
do without destroying any of it. So when I explained to him the procedure that we would
go through, like aspirating the lungs and the cavities and everything, that definitely
you would be getting body fluids. And our chemicals at that time mainly were strong
solutions of formaldehyde. And what we would do on bodies of that type that had been laying
out for several days. We, what we call VAT, we have a metal line, you know, box metal line that we put the body in and make a solution of formaldehyde and water.
It's almost straight formaldehyde and they would stay in like 19 to 24 hours. And I informed them that definitely that would alter a lot of the composition and you would lose a lot of, you know,
of the effect of the blood and all that.
Then we discussed on making the removal, how would you make a removal?
Because if a body had been laying out, like let's say in our country here,
in the summer in July, the temperatures can be anywhere from 100 to 110, 15 degrees.
The body lays out there for let's say three days.
You go to pick up the body, the tissue and everything is going to come right off in your hands.
So it's not a procedure that you can just go pick up.
So I explained that.
Did he give you any idea how long the body might have been out?
No, and I told him, I said, now listen, whatever you have, evidently you have a problem.
have the contract so I said I'd be glad to come out and see what you have and then we
could work with you. Then I could tell you how we would do it. He said no this is for
future use. He said we don't really need your service today but this is for future use.
I kind of had a suspicion that there was something because you usually don't get, you know, people
was not wanting this type of information from me. So, uh, then, uh, when I talked to him,
I said, is there a problem? If you have a problem, I thought maybe what we used to call
did you have a hot one, it was like if you had a VIP or something like that, that they
didn't want to make any announcements or anything, but also, uh, they need to determine the cause
of death and I said what you better do you better if you have a pathologist which we didn't in Roswell
at the time better call your pathologist and ask him and he'll know what you have and you better
ask him what you should do and then you better follow his procedure because otherwise you know
you could do a lot of damage to the cause of death and I said what we would probably do if
If it was something like that, if we had to take it to Albuquerque, we would probably put it in a pouch and then put some, try to freeze it immediately if possible with dry ice.
And that's probably what we would do.
He said, okay.
He said he appreciated it and that was it.
Then let's say another, probably another hour, hour and 15 minutes.
I get a call.
We had the only ambulance service.
and I got a call one emergency there was an airman that was injured in a minor accident he had a
laceration in the floor and then the nose I think he had a fractured nose and I took him to the base
but I didn't put him on a stretcher he just sat up in the front seat with me I gave him first
aid and then we just drove out to the hospital infirmary and where I usually park the
the ambulance, there was three field ambulances, old army ambulances there. And two of them,
there was an MP standing right there at the back of those field ambulances. And I really
never thought too much about it because usually there's an ambulance or something back there
most of the time anyway. But when I was taking the airmen in, we walked up on the ramp, I
I noticed the back doors, the two amulets, the field amulets were open.
I saw it looked like a wreckage.
They might have had a plane crash or something and I saw some wreckage in there.
But what I saw looked kind of like the bottom of a canoe.
It was kind of in a shape.
It reminded me, but it wasn't let's say over two feet between two and maybe possibly the
most of the pieces wouldn't be over three feet at most.
Now when you say the bottom of the canoe, did it include the curved end?
Well yes, it was part of a curve like maybe the head of the front of the canoe,
maybe just, but it was this shape, but it was kind of just on a slight curve.
but like I say, they were kind of small pieces.
How long did these objects last?
Well, they couldn't have been, they were very small pieces.
I wouldn't say that they were, they couldn't have been over maybe three feet at the most.
Anyway, there were some pieces there, and both of those kind of pieces like that,
some pretty good size, you know.
But really never thought too much about it, because when we go out on those crashes
and clean up crashes. A lot of times in the field ambulances and even in ours,
when we, a lot of times we would get a call and be there on the site before they would.
And when we've made removals of bodies or parts of it, you know, there would be a lot of dismembered
part of the bodies and some of it would be embedded into the crash, you know, into the
parts of the plane and we used to, you know, bring parts of it in and then we would take them in when
we would remove different parts of it from the crashes.
What did it appear to be made of?
Well, what it looked like to me, it looked like if you, I don't know if you've ever,
if you take stainless steel and like put a torch to it, you can see how the blue,
you'll get a blue or purplish tinge off it, you know, and it kind of looked like that.
An even color?
Well, not particularly. It was kind of modeled.
Did it exhibit gradations in color? Was it one part of the purplish stain? Was it lighter or darker?
Well, it looked like it might have been in a hot flame, so it might have looked more like stainless steel.
Most of it was kind of bluish purplish tinge that I saw.
The only difference is on this outer edge on the curve there that it looked like there
might have been some inscription or something which I kind of thought reminded me of some
Egyptian symbols or something like that.
I was walking past and I really never thought about this until I got back to the funeral.
How large were the symbols?
probably over three inches high at the most. I mean, you know, squares, but it wasn't,
as I say, these, you know, they weren't large parts, but I could definitely see that in
different shapes.
Well, did, you'd seen wreckage before, as you described.
Oh, lots of it, yeah.
Did this, what similarities did this have with the other wreckage? Was, did other wreckage
have that purplish effect you described?
Not unless you had a lot of hot fire, but usually aluminum would just melt and it wasn't
like that at all. It was just like heated stainless steel, what it looked like. Not
like burnt aluminum or anything like that. I didn't see any char, it wasn't any black
char, I didn't see anything.
Any glass windows, that type of thing?
Anything other than this particular type of metal?
No, I can't say that I saw anything different.
The letters you described, did you see them because they were painted on or because they were maybe depressed within the metal or were they raised?
It looked like they were stamped and raised, you know, it looked like you might have had a stamp that you could hit on it.
It didn't look like they were painted, it looked more or less...
Were they any color?
They were a little darker than the other, yes.
Any sign of seams on these things, rivets, screws, something that might fasten plates together?
I can't say that I did.
Okay, then what happened after you saw that?
Well, then I took the airman on in and checked him into the infirmary there and turned him over to the,
he'd have his own call, the nurses there.
And I had to always, when I'd bring him in, I'd sign a report, you know, about a funeral,
and I'd send transportation in because I'd always have to file a statement later and send him back out.
checked him in then I there was a lounge on down the hall of the ways and in the hot summer a lot
of times when you go out on a call you might be there for an hour or so and because you'd have
people on your stretchers and that your equipment would be tied up and about six miles or so in so
we usually would wait you know or if they were short of help then we would help also take the
patients off of our stretchers and get our splints and put them on x-rays and everything else so
for an hour, sometimes a couple of hours, you know, trying to help them, but mainly
you'd be wanting to get your equipment clear so you could take it on back in.
So that's the way we got acquainted with a lot of the doctors and nurses and people like
that.
So anyway, I just went back and it was hot and I thought, you know, I'd go to the lounge
and have a Coke and whoever was on duty and talk.
and there was one particular nurse that I was pretty well acquainted with, and I was going to go see if she was there, and buy her a Coke.
We usually talked a lot, but this nurse had only been there, she'd only been commissioned like around three months,
and she had graduated from college and taken the state boards and gotten her license, and then she went into the service,
was a second lieutenant. And she had started out, she came from a very deeply religious family,
Catholic, and had attended all the private preschools, Catholic schools, and all three high schools.
She wanted to be a teacher, but she, her whole thing in life was that she wanted to be a sister in none,
and she wanted to dedicate her life to God, but also helping children. She wanted to be a teacher.
But about two years after into her first two years of college, she
got this feeling, she kept saying she got this feeling from God that
he was, for some reason she always had a feeling that she should be a nurse.
So she changed her major after the first two years and then went into studying, went into the nursing training there.
And she'd given up the idea of becoming a nun?
No, that was her plan. But she wanted, what she told me that what she really wanted to do, I mean she could have stayed in the,
She could have gone on in and still gone to school and everything even though she belonged to one of the orders.
But she thought that she would better understand and everything if she went to the schools, the public schools.
And that it would help her in her teaching and then later on when she changed to nursing that she thought that she could get closer to people
people and maybe see their problems while she was young and going through training and
everything that she could if she went in in order because she would have more time to
do this. But she had nothing in mind other than never being a nun.
How old was she then?
She was 23. I was 22 and she was 23.
Go on, would you happen to remember at all where she might have graduated from?
Well, she was born and raised in St. Paul. I mean, I can't say that... I don't really know the names of the
conventions, I mean the schools or whatever she was at. I don't know that we ever discussed the names of it, other than this is what she did.
And the reason that she went into the service, she said it was kind of a burden on her parents to keep her in college.
And when she changed to nursing, then she had that opportunity to, they would pay for
the education and she would own some time afterwards.
And then as soon as she got her time served, then she would definitely go into the order
and dedicate the rest of her life to that.
But anyways, I started back to see her before I got to the, before I got back to the lounge.
There was some examining rooms on each side of the hall.
She came out of one of the examining rooms and coming across the hallway and I noticed
she had a, I don't know whether it was a handkerchief or a piece of gauze right over her mouth.
And then she saw me and she said, what are you doing here and how did you get in here?
She said, my gosh, get out of here as soon as possible.
She said, you're going to get in a lot of trouble.
And I said, what the devil's going on?
And she said, just get out of here.
And then she disappeared and that was it.
And about that time there was, when I got there right beside the door that she went in,
there was a captain standing there.
And he said, here you are. And I told him I was a Glen Denison funeral home and that I brought a patient out.
And he said, you wait here just a minute.
And he waved at someone and about that time two MPs showed up.
And where I got in trouble was I said to him, I said, looks like you had a crash.
And I said, I need to go back and get preparations ready because we usually, in a crash, we always did our identification and everything in our garages and everything.
getting the dog tags and the buddies and everything else. So I said, should I go get ready? And
he said, that's when he said, you wait right here. And then two MPs come on and said, come
on, mister, you're leaving.
What do you remember about him?
Well, I don't remember anything about him, but the two MPs was taking me down the hall.
They were on each side of me. And they told me they had orders to follow me back to the
the pinnacle. But we had gotten just, not probably over 10 or 15 feet, and then we heard
this voice that said, we're not through with that SOB. He said, bring him back. So I turned
around and went back and there was this other captain, red-headed captain. He was a mean
He looked a number, you know, but he was talking pretty rough.
And he said, you did not see anything.
There was no crash here.
You don't go into town and make any rumors that you saw anything,
that there was any crashes.
And he said, you could get in a lot of trouble.
Well, I was a little agitated, a little mad about the situation
when he called me an SOB to start with.
And I said, hey, look, mister, I'm a civilian,
and you can't do a damn thing to me.
And he said, oh yes we can mister. He said, somebody would be picking your bones out of the sand.
He said, we can do anything to you, you know, that we want to.
And then there was a sergeant, a colored sergeant, that had a pad or something in his hand, I remember that.
And he said, he'll make real good dog food. He said, he would make good dog food for our dogs.
And they said, get the SOB out. That's when they, that's when I went on out and went back to the funeral.
think, this is a novel experience, what do you think was going on?
I had no idea. I knew there was something, but at the time I didn't have any idea what
was going on. Then they did follow me all the way back to the funeral home.
Glenn, if I could backtrack one instant. Between the time that you saw the canoes,
so-called canoes, and the time that the two MPs escorted you out. Did anything else occur
during that time period that might have gotten you suspicious? Did anything else unusual
occur? Was there unusual activity? Were people running back and forth?
Well, it was unusual because I usually had a pretty free, you know, I could go in the
hospital and do whatever I wanted to. I knew a lot of the people. I never had any problem

say hi Captain and all this. We weren't out there every day. You know sometimes we'd go for a week or two and never be there. Sometimes we'd go out maybe two or three times a day. And then what happened to the airmen?
Were there any unfamiliar faces?
Oh yeah, I didn't know any of these people.
High ranking people? Any of them?
I think that Captain was probably the highest ranking one. But they were not familiar people that I'd been working with, yes.
You detect any unusual smell?
Not at that time, no. I didn't.
Then the next day, I tried to call this nurse. I wanted to call her, see what was going on.
Because then, you know, when someone escorts you back, which had never happened before, you knew there was something wrong.
It wasn't normal procedure, you knew that.
So I tried to get a hold of her and they kept telling me that she wasn't there yet.
I called maybe three or four times that morning and about 11 o'clock she called the funeral home and said,
I understand you've been trying to get a hold of him.
She said, I'm not on duty today.
But she said, I need to talk to you.
I said, fine, you want me to come to the base?
She said, well, let's just meet at the officer's club.
Because at Funilam, we had an associate membership at the officer's club.
We could go out there and use it, you know, and have the same selfies and everything,
go eat whatever we wanted to there.
We just had a more or less like a country club associate membership.
So we made this date what time we would meet, and then I went out there and I met her.
She was very upset. She looked like death had won't go.
She said, you won't believe what happened.
She said, before I talk to you, before I tell you anything,
excuse me, I'm having a throat problem here.
She said, you have to give me a sacred oath that you will not ever mention my name.
She said, you can get me in a lot of trouble.
what I'm going to tell you, you don't know where you got this, you know."
And I said, what do you mean by sacred oath?
And she said, I mean like cutting your arm off, that's what she told me.
And I said, okay, because I said I would definitely like to know what's going on.
Do you think she was telling you this because you were good friends?
Oh, I think so, and I think she didn't want to get in trouble either
because she was very conscientious of everything. I mean, the rules and regulations, I mean, that was just like reading her Bible.
You know, you followed the rules and regulations.
Yet, she told you.
She didn't have to say anything.
And that probably was against the rules, wasn't it? Telling you?
Well, sure. I would assume, she wouldn't have told me that unless someone said, you keep this to yourself or whatever. I'm assuming this now.
But anyway, she said, what happened, the way she got involved in the first place, she was going across the room to this other room to pick up some supplies.
This is where the two doctors that were in there supposedly doing a preliminary autopsy on these bodies.
And she got whatever she went and she started out and these doctors said,
you're not going anywhere, we have to have you and you.
We have to have some help.
And she said she never smelled anything so horrible in her life when she got in there.
And I said it was the most gruesome, most horrible sight that she'd ever seen in her life. The smell was almost devastating. She said, I was never so horrified in my life.
And she said, I don't know if I'll ever sleep again or anything else. She said, I've never seen anything so gruesome.
I said, well look, you're a nurse and I said, anytime you're in this business you're going to see a lot of things.
And I said, you may as well get used to it. And she said, no, this is what it is. She said, this is something that no one's ever seen.
Was she ordinarily calm or emotional?
Oh no, she was so hysterical that she would grab—
Calmly ordinarily?
Yeah, well, yes. She was very, not laid back, but very precise though. She would grab her head and shake her head and cover her eyes and everything else.
What were you thinking at this point?

Well, I didn't know because I was thinking that she was going into total shock. I really thought, hey, there's a problem here. And I thought she would probably go into total shock is what I really think.
And while she was telling this, other people were there in the…
There wasn't anyone around us because we kind of had a table up on the side of the
officer club ourselves. And she was hoping that no one could hear us. In fact, there
was some up maybe at the counter there, we took the bar there, we were in the lounge
and we had ordered a sandwich. And, uh, but she was never, never touched her sandwich
I don't think I ever did either, I'm not sure.
But she looked like she was going in this total shock, really.
And I said, my God, you know.
And she said, I have a, she said, last night I made a diagram.
She said, you won't believe this, but she said, I made a diagram.
And she said, these little bodies.
And she gave me a, she drew me a diagram of an arm.
because she said the anatomy from the shoulder to here was real short and this arm was longer here.
There was only four fingers on, there wasn't a thumb, only four fingers.
Little long, very fragile little hands.
She said when one of the hands was detached from the arm, and she said when the doctors turned it over,
that she noticed something, and they did, they made a notation.
That's what she was doing, was trying to take notes and making notations for them.
And they were all sick. But she said that on the tips of these little fingers,
they looked like little pads with little holes that kind of looked like a small suction cup
on each end of these fingers here. She said there was no thumb at all on that,
they only had like the four fingers on that. And she said the heads were very much larger
than the body. It was out of proportion for the size of the body they had. The eyes were
very deeply set back and set in. And she said the amazing thing about the skulls that it
wasn't like ours, that it was kind of like a newborn baby. They were kind of flexible
that, you know, the doctors couldn't move, that it wasn't, you know, like a hard skull.
She said that was a different, the nose was very concave. She said it was only like a couple of little orifices.
And you didn't have the bridge of the nose, but it was more or less concave.
The mouth was just a real fine little slit there.
The doctor said there was no teeth, but it looked like maybe a heavy cartilage or something like that.
it was very kind of hard, but not like, you know, whizzing teeth or anything. The ears,
they had, the ears didn't have any, there wasn't an ear like ours, but there was a couple of little
orifices in the ears up here on each side. Very small, but it looked like there was a couple of
little, like little flaps, she explained it. And she drew me a diagram of the head, she drew me a
diagram of the arms and the hands. And it was on the back of a prescription pad where,
you know, the nurses always carried a prescription pad, you know, and I'll take the notes and
everything for the doctors and all that. These were rather small, but she had drawn those
the night before. And she gave them to me. She said, you know, you can have these, but
there again, I was sworn to secrecy again that, you know, either destroy them after
I got through with them, whatever.
Anything about these beans, their necks?
She didn't say anything about the necks. She didn't say anything about the clothing.
She said that they definitely had no hair at all.
But then about that time, she said they all became so very ill.
And when I saw her coming out, that's when she was so sick she thought she was going to vomit.
What were they old from?
Well, mainly from the odor, I think. She said it was the most cut off smell that she'd ever smelled in her life.
Of course, being in the funeral bed, she said I smelled floaters and everything else. I mean, I've been through that experience and I know what she was talking about.
Now, how many bodies were there?
She said there was three bodies. Two of them were very mangled. She said it looked like some predatory or something might have been destroying portions of the bodies
The tissue and some of it were cut in strings like you know they were pulled.
The doctors thought maybe this is what happened.
But some of them, like she said, the hands and the arms were all dismembered from,
of course that could have happened from the removal, you don't know what happened.
One she said was really pretty much all there and this was one that they were describing, you know.

She said the body was well intact, that one was. She said they were like between three and a half to four feet tall, so that would give you, but the bodies were black. Of course, you know, being exposed to the helmet could have caused that.
How did she refer to them? What did she call them?
She didn't know what to call them. She just said small bodies, that's to my knowledge now. I don't think she ever called them anything except very small bodies.
Did she express any idea of what their origin was?
The doctor said it, the two doctors, and she didn't know whether they were pathologists or what, but she had never seen them before either.
And so she assumed they might be pathologists, but she wasn't sure.
No, I mean the bodies.
But she said the doctors, what again, she said the doctors said, hey this isn't anything we've ever seen before in our life,
and there's no textbooks that ever covered this.
Is there any indication of sex of these beings?
I asked her about that and she said, I don't know.
She said, I didn't look and I don't think anybody else did.
She said that two of their bodies were probably so mangled
that they probably couldn't have told it.
She said, I don't know about the other one.
Did she say anything about legs, feet?
She didn't.
What she diagrammed and what she told me about the head and the arms and the hands
Then she got real ill again while we were sitting there and she said,
she said, I've got to get back to the barracks.
She said, I just can't. She said, I don't think I can make it another step.
Anyway, I drove her. We went to the officer club and I drove her back to the barracks there,
to the nurses' quarters.
That was the last time I ever saw her.
The next day I called.
I called out and started calling her the next day to just see mainly how she was.
She, they just said that she wasn't available and I called back later. I called all that
day and I never did get her. Then I called back the next day and when I called the next
day, one of the nurses... What would they say when you would call?
They just said she's not here, that she's not on duty today is what they really said.
The next day I called and I got one of the nurses that I was familiar with, but I can't remember her name either. I didn't remember her name.
She said, she said, she's not here. She said she's been transferred out. And I said, really? And she said, yeah.
She said, she and several of the other personnel have been transferred out.
She said, I don't know anything, I can't tell you more than that, and that's all I know.
So I got maybe a week, maybe ten days, or let's say two weeks, ten days to two weeks, I'm not sure at the time.
I got this letter, and all that was in the letter was that she said that this was my APO number.
She said, I don't have time to write or anything right now, but this is an APO number you can address a letter to.
And she said, we will discuss this in a letter on what happened later on.
Something, I mean, don't hold me word to word, but this was the gist of it.
Very short, just a note.
And said, but I am in London.
And that was it.
So I write a letter to her and that was sent just to the battery fueling browser.
So then I think the next day or something I sit down and I wrote her a letter hoping that she wasn't in any problem and having any problem.
I was hoping that she got over the shock and everything and the trauma that she'd been through.
and about two weeks, I'd say it was at least two weeks or more, the letter that I had sent come back and said return to sender.
Then on the corner down in red letters it said deceased. And that was it. That was my letter that was sent back to the funeral home there.
Stamps on the letter? It was stamped deceased. It was in a red block.
Did you ask anybody at the base?
Oh yeah, I didn't. Well I guess two or three weeks went by, but I didn't go out. Like I said, we didn't go every day, but every time I'd go out I'd say,
Lieutenant. Finally one of the ladies said, well the rumor is, she said this is strictly a rumor,
I can't confirm anything else, but the rumor is that she and five other nurses were on a training
mission and they went down and they were all killed in a plane crash. And she said that's
all I know and that's all I can tell you. So then I never did hear anymore, but I kept asking did
you ever, you know every once in a while I'd go out and I'd say, did anybody ever heard,
I don't even know about the crash or anything and no one had ever heard anything. That was the last I ever heard.
But you never got any official word?
No, no, no. So that was pretty much my involvement in this.
Glenn, the next time you had occasion to go out to the base, was everything normal?
Pretty much so.
Were they treating you normally?
Pretty much so, but there were some new faces around, yes. But everything was pretty normal.
Were there some old faces missing?
Oh yeah, some. But another thing going back to the, when the doctors, she and the doctors became very ill.
And she said that they didn't finish the autopsies or anything right there, that they couldn't take it any longer.
And they had the old air conditioner, you know, and the smell was so bad that they were afraid this was going to go through the ducts
and they would go through the rest of the hospital into the other room.
So she said they came in and they made a removal
and they took the bodies to one of the hangars to finish the work over there.
But she didn't go with them?
Oh, no, no.
Were there any other nurses assisting?
No, she was the only one.
How many doctors were normally on the base staff?
What do you think?
I don't really know how many was on the staff,
You know when you'd go out there, there was always a doctor or nurse that was on call and all the chefs.
She had a lot of orderlies back in those days. You'd have corpus and everybody doing all the big pan work, you know, and the cleaning and all this kind of business.
Did they ever make that order for the caskets?
No, never did. Never heard any more about it.
Did you hear anything at all from the military about keeping quiet?
No, just the time that I was threatened there in the hull of this captain and this sergeant,
the only time that I was ever...
So there was no follow up?
No, and then another thing, I'd forgotten, the next day when the sheriff and my father,
Sheriff Wilcox, were very close friends. My father was kind of an old gunsman, he was
but he would make special stocks for different people in town, you know,
and their guns and their rifles and all that.
He and the sheriff were pretty good,
and they used to play down those once in a while on Saturday evening or something.
And the sheriff went to my folks' house the next morning.
Next morning after what?
After I was threatened, you know.
And he went to the house, and he wanted to talk to my father,
and he said, I don't know what kind of trouble Glenn's in out at the base,
but he said evidently he's a problem.
But he said, I've come out to tell him, to tell you, to you tell your son,
that whatever he does, that he didn't know anything,
he didn't see anything that happened at the base.
And he said, I don't know what, George said, I don't know what the problem is,
but he said they want the names, they want you and your wife's name,
and they want all your children's names and addresses.

And my father, he said, you know, he said, well, until I know why, he said, I don't think it's any of their damn business, whatever it is. But he said, I, he said, my son, he said, we raised our children that, you know, they were to do right.
He said, I can't believe we've gotten in any trouble.
So he drove me to the funeral home.
And he came in and he said, son, what kind of trouble are you in out at the base?
And I said, I'm not in any trouble.
And he said, I can't help you if you don't tell me the truth.
And I said, Dad, I'm not in any trouble.
I said, I know I'm not.
He said, well, George Wilcox told me that you might be in some trouble.
So I knew that he wasn't going to leave or leave me alone until I told him.
And this is the only man that I've ever told this story to until I told Stanton Freeman one day.
When I told him what the problem was and that I'd been threatened, he became very upset.
And he thought, well, he might just go get his gun and settle some things.
He was very upset about it because, you know, if I'd have done anything I would have paid the price with him before anything else because that's the way we were raised.
But he became very upset. But he's the only man I ever told. And I told him to don't ever repeat this to anyone, not that I was particularly afraid.
What was his reaction when you told him?
Well, he was just very upset, very mad.
No, I don't mean about you being told to shut up. Did you tell him the full story?
I told him, yeah, pretty much this is what I told you. And he said, oh hell, maybe you shouldn't tell the story.
He said, I don't know. I don't know what to do about this. And I said, well, just keep your mouth shut, I guess.
That's what they want me to do. But it really didn't bother me. I was upset and mad because I didn't like them going in there and calling me names.
If they would have said, hey, this is some emergency, I mean, national security or whatever.
Because, you know, back in those days, everybody's patriotism was high back in the 40s, you know,
and second after the war.
And if they would have got to threaten and everything else, it was a little difficult.
And I just told them, go to hell.
And I really, I guess I was too stupid to really be scared.
You know, I wasn't really afraid they were going to do it.
How do you know? I think a lot of other people who tried to tell us that.
Glenn, what did you think when perhaps that day or the next day or whenever the article
came out in the newspaper about the Army Air Force picking up the wreckage of so-called
flying disks? You connected those in your mind?
Well, I did then.
What did you think?
Well, then I figured then that what the lieutenant of the bodies that she worked on had to be
naturally, you know, it was quite a bit of talk around town for a few days after that.
A lot of people didn't believe it. A lot of them thought it was scientific experiments
from different, you know, the Army or the Air Force or somebody had it or whatever.
A lot of people didn't take it really serious and thought it would be it.
You would just keep mumbling when somebody talked to you about it?
tough for me. You know, even Walter and I have been friends. I've known a lot of these people,
Wilcox and all of us, you know. And I see back in those days we didn't have corners. I mean,
we didn't have a corner per se, but we had corners in the inquest. And we would have
homicides or suicides or fatalities or whatever. And most of the time I was on the, I would be,
you know, a witness or what. I was in bombing the bodies and working on them. I'd have to go testify to the cause of death and all this.
And so I was with the sheriff a lot. And we never discussed this. Even the deputies never discussed this. No one ever discussed it.
Walter and I have known Fred and been social friends for years. None of us until, you know, two years ago. But I never said anything.
It wasn't that I was trying to hide anything or whatever they were talking.
After I saw how Walter and everybody was getting involved, I said,
I don't know whether I want to get involved or not, but my wife is one that talks me into it.
She said, well, I think you ought to at least get your story on the record.
She said it may not mean anything, but at least get it on the record
and then tell everybody to leave you alone and go on your way.
She said, I think you should do that. That's the only reason that I did, was just because she thought maybe I should.
I didn't know if it was important or not. Anyway, Stan Friedman had been after me, and Bob Shirky brought Stan up that day.
Kay said, I'll go ahead and get it to him, and get it out of the way, and forget about it.
Well, looking back to that time in 1947, what do you think was going on?
Well, you know, certainly none of us had ever heard of the UFO or aliens or anything else.
The only thing we heard anything even close to that was a Washington, W. radio program, you know, back in time.
I never thought anything about it. I was out at the base a lot, around the military. My brother was a fighter pilot and all this.
I was there during the war because I was 4F. I only had one ear. That's why I'm having to sit sideways to you to understand you.
but I never really thought anything about it really.
After that I've never thought too much about it.
I don't think any of us ever thought too much about it.
How do you feel now about the military's behavior and the whole thing?
Well, my mind was made up when they threatened me that day that,
okay, I think, you know, so what are you trying to cover up?
Tell us the truth and we'll either keep our mouths shut and go on our way or forget about it.
But you don't like to be called names, you don't like to be threatened. I mean, that's only human nature, you know, none of us like to be threatened.
So I was upset about it, yeah, and I was real mad about it. At the time I got over it.
Then I was really concerned when I never heard from the lieutenant again. I still think to this day that she, this is strictly my, what I think now.
Knowing her and everything, knowing that she wanted to go back in, she wanted to join the
Order, she wanted to be, you know, to help. Mainly she wanted to be in Children's, to
help the young children and all this. I think they probably discharged her and put her in
the government somewhere. I think that's where she's been all these years. I'm just thinking
it. I don't think she was ever killed. I don't think so.
Glenn, the drawings, could you talk about them, where they might be today? I've heard

them? Well Stan and I had a file. I'm a nut on filing everything. And I had a personal file, but I also had a file at the funeral home. I kept a file in the history of all the suicides, of everything that I was involved in. I always kept a record myself. Because I was the one at the funeral home that would always have to go to the inquest and everything.
And then you always had insurance companies, you always had families that would come back
and maybe two or three years later.
And I always made it even, I was so precise that I even wrote what kind of clothes everybody
could, you'd get letters, you know, three or four years later, my husband or my son
that was killed there in a certain day, he'd had on a certain jacket and all that.
What did you do with it and all that.
So I had real good records.
When Stan was there, and I left the funeral home, the reason I left, because I bought a funeral home myself, and I bought a funeral home and I went into business for myself.
And I didn't go after, I didn't think to get my records, because there was a lot of the records that I wanted, you know, that I would like, that was personal, that I would like.
and I even had the letter in there from her that I kept those.
But when Stan and I, we found the old, and I had it down in the basement, we found the old filing cabinet,
and we found it, we didn't, but what had happened, all of those old military files,
I even had all the records for the ambulances. I mean, we had ambulances, everything was separated.
And I could go back and tell you when we took to the hospital and the time and everything else.
All those records were destroyed. They just took the whole thing out of the files to make room for it.
And they just took them out to the city dump and threw them away.
Were any of your files still there?
All my files were in there.
Were any of your files still there?
No.
They were all gone.
Stan and I, we found it. Just like I explained to you in the filing cabinet.
One of the boys that I'd hired before Edwin, the husband of the funeral home that I'd hired,
records out and he told Stan, he said, well I remember Glenn's records but I didn't think
they were you know worth anything. He said I personally carried them up you know and took them out.
And that's probably where the drawings were. Yeah. I made a drawing I think,
I don't know maybe you guys have seen it, I don't know, but I made a drawing the best of my knowledge
of what she gave me you know and that was the best that I could remember and the best I could do and
and I didn't make that drawing, but she gave me.
This officer who had you removed, did you ever see him again?
No, never did see him again.
Any clues to where he might have come from?
The only thing that I've ever heard about it was Stan Friedman called me.
One time Stan called me and he was very excited. He said that he had just interviewed someone,
some young boy, a kid or somebody that was hypnotized. He explained the red-headed
officer and also the black sergeant. He called me, he was so excited about it. He said,
I always told Stan it was the meanest looking eyes that I'd ever seen on a man and he said this kid explained the same thing to him.
He was real excited, cool, thank you very much.
But I never did see him after that.
Anyway, that's the way I was involved in this.
When did you leave the Ballard Funeral Home?
It was about, I think in the early 60's.
And what was your position at the time?
I was manager.
Mr. Ballard was still there, but he was the mayor and he was involved in local politics and everything else.
So I pretty well managed everything. I never really had a title as manager, I just automatically did everything, made all the decisions, did all the ordering.
It wasn't, you know, Roswell's small, he just didn't have funerals every day and everything.
Did you still have the base contract?
Yeah, we had the base contract all the time it was there.
Did you get the base contract then when you opened your own?
No, I didn't have it at all.
But, you know, they closed the base. I don't remember what year they closed it, but they closed the base.
We just automatically got it. Politics, that's what the mayor knew and they would let you
go. That's politics for you.
It doesn't change.
Do you think of anything else?
Any contact with the lieutenant's parents? Did she have parents?
I never had any contact. I had contact one time that I was out there and she introduced
me to a brother. She said, I want you to meet my brother Bill. And he was a sergeant, but
I don't think he was in the Air Force. I think he was in the Army or something.
Would they have any knowledge other than yours of her disappearance?
Well, see I never contacted any of them after that. I never heard from anyone after that.
He was just like her. He wanted to serve his country, but he was also studying to be a priest.
And he wanted to, after the service, he wanted to go in and be a priest.
It was a very developed family. They were really something else.
Glenn, were the MPs on the base and the guards running around with rifles and unholstered
weapons?
Well, they always had a pistol in on their belt.
They didn't have them drawn or anything?
No, no, no.
Was there any sign of increased security?
Well, the only thing I noticed was standing back at those ambulances, and I don't know
they were supposed to be a garden or what. But certainly I'd never seen any MPs before and certainly there was never any MPs escort us back to the pin loan.
But I really never noticed any at the time that I was involved in it. I just told you the MPs that I was involved with and that's all that I can say that I ever saw.
How long were you in the building?
Oh, I couldn't have been there. They didn't let me stay in there very long. I probably wasn't in there over 15 minutes. I'm just guessing something like 15-20 minutes at the most.
And until this officer spotted you, nobody gave you a hard time?
No, because she was upset because I was there and now I got in. That was unusual. She was hysterical then. How did you get in here? Get out as soon as you're going to get in a lot of trouble.
But it wasn't a normal day in the base hospital, I can tell you that. It wasn't even normal.
Because we were never threatened. We pretty well had a run in the base. No one ever stopped us.
We were out there in the ambulance. We were there. We buried all the dependents, you know, the military dependents,
and babies and everything else, tail horns. We were involved out there quite intimately.
So we didn't ever have any problems. No one ever questioned us when we were out there
about what we were doing. We worked with the chaplains real well.
It would seem that you were accorded a great deal of respect then by the military for the
dog you were doing.
Oh yeah, and the MBC—
They appreciated what you were doing.

When we would go out on the, back in those days, every time you'd go out on an emergency, the MPs and the police, when we, before we ever left Funilon, we called the police station and said we have an emergency at whatever address we were going to.
They would dispatch a car there and they would always meet us there.
At that time an MP would always ride with one of the, when we had the military base,
it would always be, most of the time the MPs would ride with one of the policemen.
You got a military, you got an MP, military police along with the others.
And they were most out there.
And we worked real good with them and they were all pretty good guys.
In fact, there's several of those MPs today that they're retired from the police force
in Roswell. Stayed in Roswell, married Roswell girls. We had a real good relation with the
base. That was the only time we ever had any problems.
One day, essentially.
Well I guess that covers it then. Certainly appreciate you taking your time. We'll see
what comes of this.
